author: Brooke Siem
title: The Episode: A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing – A Conversation With Mary Ann Kenny
content:
W

elcome to the Mad in America podcast. My name is Brooke Siem, and I am the author of the award-winning memoir on antidepressant withdrawal, 

May Cause Side Effects

.




Today I am with Mary Ann Kenny. Mary Ann is an academic, and she lives in Dublin with her children. She is the author of the book, 

The Episode: A True Story of Loss, Madness and Healing

.




In her book, Mary Ann details her descent into psychosis, her hopitalization, and her journey back to health and happiness. Drawing on her detailed medical files and on her own recollections, she has created a day-by-day account of what it is like to lose touch with reality while dealing with grief and living in the dreadful knowledge that everything you care about in life is under threat.




The transcript below has been edited for length and clarity. Listen to the audio of the interview here.

author: Jordyn Tovey
title: What Would Marsha Linehan Do?
content:
Over the past few weeks, the world has shown up to mourn and honor the impact of Marsha Linehan. And I among them.

I had the formative experience of interning at a DBT clinic in Michigan on my way to becoming a licensed clinical social worker and psychotherapist. I spent over a year learning, teaching, and practicing the “gold standard” treatment.

Now, years later, I find that the tenets, theoretical formulation, skills, and dare I say, spirit of DBT have remained with me. As have the questions which ultimately led me away from practicing in a full-fidelity setting.

I struggled at the time to put words to my Catholic upbringing (and subsequent rebellion) rearing its head. Now, in her death, I am reminded of the peculiarities of what it was like to hear Marsha Linehan’s name invoked in clinical spaces.

For example, in required consultation, there would be callbacks to things Marsha had said and done in demonstrations to guide the therapist, rather than grounding in the individual, totally separate relationship of therapist and client. Dialectical behavior therapists practicing true to the texts are encouraged to borrow directly from Marsha’s style. Her cadence. Her turns of phrase. Her irreverence. Her intensity. Ask themselves the question: what would Marsha do?

author: Kristopher Drummond
title: Therapy as Rite of Passage Pt. 2: Cultivating Secure Attachment to the Earth
content:
Photo courtesy of the author.




Therapy, in its crazy way, by emphasizing the inner soul and 

ignoring the outer soul, supports the decline of the actual world

. Yet therapy goes on blindly believing that it’s curing the outer world by making better people. We’ve had that for years and years: “If everybody went into therapy, we’d have better buildings, we’d have better people, we’d have more consciousness.” 

It’s not the case

.




—James Hillman




W

e know—

we know—

that the future our imaginations were promised is not the future that awaits us. This summer, more than any previous, is our evidence. As I write, fires rage across the American west, bombs drop on children, surveillance architecture is daily being constructed outside rural convenience stores. In our hearts, if we look, the knowing of where we really are is clear.




For many in the West, the future has long been a source of secure attachment. It has been our god, a shining destination justifying the sacrifices of generations. All the brutality of history has supposedly made sense through the lens of progress. 

We’re going somewhere amazing. 

Utopia has been just around the corner with every technological advance, asking for just a bit more patience, a bit more sacrifice, a bit more relinquishment of our humanity—just enough so that when the robots take our jobs, the foretold dawning of endless leisur

author: S.C.
title: Haldol First, Questions Later: My Psychiatric Detention
content:
T

his is not a post I wanted to write. I wanted to be able to go through my psychiatric admission patient file and affirm that healthcare providers definitively met their duty to the standard of care, and hewed as closely as possible to their Hippocratic oaths — within reason, of course. I wanted to be able to affirm that any initial feelings I had of betrayal and victimization were likely just figments of an overactive imagination, and potentially even evocative of a budding persecutory delusional disorder, and I should do my best to banish the thought.




But I can’t.




As the documents slowly trickled in from my family physician (because the hospital never provided any to me directly, despite my pleas), those feelings only deepened. Something monstrous really did happen to me in April of 2026. Doctors didn’t just breach the standard of care, but brazenly, maliciously, perhaps even gleefully continued to traumatize me, time and time again. This was not care. This was its evil twin: harm.

author: Alan Robinson
title: The Right to Irrationally Refuse Treatment: An Interview with Ron Thompson
content:
Editor’s Note: This Mad in the World report features an interview with activist and attorney Ron Thompson, interviewed by Locura en Argentina founder Alan Robinson.

From serving on the boards of the American Civil Liberties Union and the Bazelon Center, and participating in advocacy initiatives supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, to collaborating with pioneering figures like Judi Chamberlin, Loren Mosher, and Thomas Szasz, Ron Thompson has been an incisive observer of the psychiatric survivor movement since 1986. Here, he speaks from a very lucid and provocative perspective about the systemic flaws of biological psychiatry, the limits of legal reform, and why guaranteeing the right to refuse treatment on irrational grounds remains the final frontier for patient autonomy.

Ron Thompson: Thank you for the introduction, Alan. I am glad to be here.

Thompson: My introduction in 1986 was truly a revelation. By chance, I came across an article in the Washington Post that mentioned someone I recognized from my prep school days at Phillips Exeter Academy. The article concerned St. Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, D.C.—a psychiatric facility and prison. We had been on the same wrestling team together years prior.

I decided to track him down. When I visited him at St. Elizabeths, I was astounded by his condition and the stark contrast between his life and mine. Physically, it was obvious that his incarceration and treatment had severely damaged him. He was overweight, and his skin tone was unnatural. While he held unconventional ideas—he was the son of a prominent financial figure and imagined arranging grand financial deals between China and the United States—his thoughts made a distinct kind of sense when understood within his personal history.

We formed an immediate connection. Because he could not leave on his own, I was granted permission to take him off hospital grounds for meals at a nearby Chinese restaurant. Spending time with him made me realize how extraordinarily fortunate I had been 20 years earlier during my own encounter with the psychiatric system. When I was hospitalized decades prior. I was hospitalized as a voluntary patient, a status retained throughout my connection to the McLean Hospital near Boston, Mass in the town of Belmont.

Thompson: Many years have passed, but the treatment must have lasted approximately two and a half years. I entered the hospital in November, 1964 after a few weeks into my first semester at Georgetown University Law Center in Washington DC, when I woke up one morning and, according to memory, couldn’t see myself in the mirror. I called my parents and abruptly returned to their home in Dover, New Hampshire.

After what may have been only a few weeks, I told the doctors I was feeling sicker. Most remarkable of all their decisions, they decided that this was because of the drugs I was on, either Haldol or Thorazine, or both of them. And 3 or 4 months later, I told the doctors that I had to leave in-patient status or “something bad would happen,” whatever I meant by that. Again, the doctors made a remarkable decision, and said “ok,” despite that somewhat ominous phrase.

To summarize my treatment, it might be enough to say that my sickness was primarily due to a mother, who was not abusive in any ordinary way, but whose lifelong anxiety, combined with erratic and sudden emotional changes, and perhaps also with the example or ‘lesson’ of a father who lived with this difficult woman by more or less pretending no problem existed, led me to conclude that radical suppression of emotion was the way to deal with any and all kinds of emotional discomfort.

Thompson: It has now been 40 years since I began this work in 1986. My connection with NIMH began shortly after I got involved in advocacy. At the time, Joe Rogers—a prominent and dynamic figure in the movement—had visited me after I wrote a somewhat satirical piece about his style. Despite the critique, he engaged with me respectfully, and through those networks, I was introduced to a small, progressive unit within NIMH.

This unit was experimentation-oriented. They were boldly attempting to fund patient advocates and former patients to participate in national dialogues. NIMH began sponsoring my travel to conferences across the United States and even internationally, including a conference in Finland.

This support allowed me to engage with almost every major figure in the movement. I established a close dialogue with Thomas Szasz, worked alongside Peter Breggin, and co-led a workshop with Loren Mosher, the founder of Soteria House. The leadership at NIMH’s advocacy unit was genuinely supportive. However, the relationship between government funding and radical activism is inherently complex. While federal sponsorship provided essential resources and a platform, grassroots movements always face the risk of co-optation when working within state-funded structures.

Thompson: Loren Mosher and I shared a fundamental agreement: the dominant psychiatric paradigm was deeply broken. Soteria House proved that compassionate, non-coercive community support without heavy reliance on neuroleptics could yield superior long-term outcomes.

Regarding terminology, language was constantly debated—whether to use “ex-patients,” “psychiatric survivors,” or “consumers.” But my legal background led me to focus on a deeper conceptual issue beyond terminology. Although I graduated from law school and passed the bar, I chose not to enter traditional fee-for-service practice, retaining instead the analytical mindset of an attorney.

I have always been skeptical of how “patient rights” are framed. In standard medicine, every competent human being possesses the legally protected right to make what society might consider an “irrational refusal” of medical treatment in other people’s eyes. For instance, Steve Jobs famously delayed surgical treatment for his cancer in favor of alternative therapies. Similarly, former Oregon Senator Wayne Morse refused life-sustaining dialysis. Society may view such decisions as unwise, but the law respects personal bodily autonomy.

In psychiatry, however, this fundamental right does not exist. The moment a person’s decision is deemed “irrational” due to supposed mental illness, their right to refuse treatment is stripped away. Therefore, campaigning for minor “patient rights”—like better hospital food or phone access—without securing the fundamental right to refuse treatment remains inherently incomplete.

Thompson: When I speak of an “unreasonable refusal” I mean a refusal that appears irrational in other people’s eyes, like observers or clinicians. To illustrate this, I wrote an essay titled A Tale of Two Patients.

It details the story of a close friend whose authoritarian parents had him involuntarily committed and subjected to physical restraints and forced drugging, despite him not being mentally ill. I supported his legal fight, and eventually, the hospital conceded and released him. Although he was vindicated, the physical trauma, dental neglect, and severe insomnia resulting from his institutionalization permanently hindered his ability to reintegrate into society. I have remained in contact with him weekly for over 30 years; he remains sane, yet severely disabled by the system that claimed to treat him.

This highlights what I call the “zero-sum fallacy” in psychiatry. Society operates under the assumption that if Person A is exhibiting unusual or disturbing behavior, then Person B (the psychiatrist) automatically knows what is best to do. The first premise may be true—someone may indeed be in distress—but the second premise is false.

If an individual poses an imminent physical threat to themselves or others, society may choose to intervene for public safety. However, that intervention must be recognized for what it is: a state security measure, not a medical treatment. Labeling involuntary confinement and forced drugging as “medical care” degrades the true meaning of medicine.

Thompson: In the early 1990s, a colleague and I organized a debate at St. Elizabeths Hospital. During that presentation, I proposed an alternative model for psychiatric wards.

I argued that if society deems it necessary to confine an individual for safety reasons, institutional staff should be entirely honest with that person. They should say: “We do not have a medical cure for your distress, but society has mandated that you cannot leave right now. Given this reality, how can we work together as fellow human beings to make your stay tolerable and help you regain your independence?”

This approach respects the individual’s humanity. It eliminates the deception of pretending that forced drugging is a therapeutic gift. Honesty creates a foundation for genuine dialogue, whereas forced medicalization creates hostility and trauma.

Thompson: In 1971, I decided to return to law school; by then I was already married to my first wife. I had a vague sense that ‘something’ wasn’t quite right with my emotional make-up, a feeling that came to the surface of my consciousness in the spring of 1974, when I had the unsettling experience of being unable to complete my final law school exams. It wasn’t because I didn’t know the answers, but because passing meant I would have to go out and find a job working for other people, and my subconscious flatly refused to allow it.

In any case, a very wise friend who was a professor told me that I ‘of course’ ought to go back and finish that final semester, which I did; I graduated and then sat and passed the bar exam.

But I realized I was incapable of wanting to work for someone else, which, over time, I came to understand was due to my inability to access the emotion of anger. This may sound strange, but in a way, accessing this emotion also means accessing the emotions necessary for self-assertion when you are in a subordinate position. It’s hard to explain.

Thompson: Well, it’s a problem that’s continuing, and I have to say it’s also society’s problem. I don’t want to put it all on the ex-patients. The challenge lies both in strategic miscalculations within advocacy movements and in society’s deep desire for simple answers.

A clear example occurred in 1993 during the national debate over health insurance parity. There was a major legislative push to mandate equal insurance coverage for physical and mental health conditions. I argued at the time that survivor organizations should only support parity if it was strictly limited to voluntary psychiatric care.

However, many mainstream advocacy groups decided to compromise. They believed that achieving broad parity first was paramount, assuming they could address the problem of involuntary coercion later. By securing insurance parity without excluding coercive practices, the movement inadvertently legitimized involuntary psychiatry. Insurance companies were now obligated to fund forced hospitalizations and chemical restraints. Compromising on core principles weakened the movement’s moral clarity, leaving the general public unaware of the fundamental distinction between consensual care and psychiatric coercion.

Thompson: While these cases established important procedural hurdles, they did not dismantle the underlying structure of involuntary psychiatry. Courts created procedural checks, but they ultimately left authority in the hands of administrative bodies and medical professionals.

The legal system lacks a specific civil tort tailored to remedy psychiatric abuse. Standard tort law—such as battery or medical malpractice—is routinely bypassed when courts grant broad immunity to psychiatrists acting under state civil commitment statutes. Litigation can chip away at extreme abuses, such as solitary confinement, but legal reform alone cannot dismantle a paradigm that society relies upon to manage social distress.

Thompson: Biological psychiatry claims that complex emotional suffering and behavioral distress are simply “brain diseases” or “chemical imbalances.” This concept is scientifically unproven, yet it remains enormously seductive for several reasons.

First, it appeals to psychiatrists. For decades, psychoanalysts and talking therapists faced skepticism from mainstream medicine. By rebranding emotional suffering as a biological disease, psychiatrists could claim status as “real physicians” prescribing biological cures.

Second, it appeals to patients and families looking for relief. Accepting a biological diagnosis removes personal responsibility and guilt. It offers a quick fix: take a pill to manage symptoms.

However, symptom management is not recovery. When I was hospitalized, my doctor told me something psychiatrists rarely say today: “You are going to be better than well.” They meant I could understand the root causes of my breakdown, grow through the experience, and emerge stronger than before. Modern biological psychiatry has abandoned the pursuit of genuine healing in favor of lifelong pharmaceutical management.

Thompson: My recovery was made possible by a combination of empathetic clinical care, meaningful human relationships, supportive family, and personal reflection.

First, my psychoanalysts treated me with profound respect. They listened when I reported that medication was making me sicker, discontinued the drugs, and allowed me to retain my dignity. Though I was in a locked ward, I wore a coat and tie and was permitted to leave the hospital grounds.

Second, solidarity with fellow patients was crucial. I formed deep friendships with two older patients—a traumatized Vietnam veteran dealing with severe anxiety, and a man from New York suffering from deep depression. The three of us spent hours talking and supporting one another. That peer connection provided comfort that no medication could offer.

Third, my father provided unwavering support. For nearly two years following my breakdown, he enabled me to commute 75 miles round-trip three times a week for outpatient psychoanalysis.

Fourth, the clinical team demonstrated extraordinary trust. During my recovery, my mother—acting out of intense anxiety—found a small souvenir starter pistol I had purchased years earlier during a road trip and frantically called the hospital, claiming I was dangerous. When I met with the doctors, I calmly explained the situation. Instead of panicking or re-institutionalizing me, they believed me. That vote of confidence was transformative.

Finally, intellectual study guided my healing. I immersed myself in the works of psychoanalyst Harry Stack Sullivan, who distinguished between objective fear and rootless anxiety often absorbed from an anxious environment. I read Karen Horney, particularly her masterpiece Neurosis and Human Growth, which provided a roadmap for understanding self-realization. I also studied Abraham Maslow, who shifted psychology’s focus away from pathology toward studying self-actualized, psychologically healthy individuals. These thinkers provided the conceptual tools I needed to rebuild my life.

Thompson: I would encourage young advocates to cultivate deep introspection and distinguish between two fundamentally different ways of being: possessing a strong sense of self versus possessing a strong ego.

A strong sense of self is grounded in internal values, self-awareness, reason, and empathy. Consider Abraham Lincoln. He possessed an extraordinary sense of self—he was reflective, capable of deep empathy, and guided by principle. In contrast, a strong ego is fragile, defensive, and pathologically self-centered, demanding constant validation while lacking empathy.

Effective advocacy requires emotional maturity. Activists must learn to distinguish between genuine, constructive emotions and neurotic, reactive drives. They must also seek out wise mentors. Peer support is vital, but learning from older generations who have navigated these struggles provides invaluable perspective.

In my own youth, my role model was my YMCA camp director, Oscar Elwell. He embodied calm authority without a trace of authoritarianism. He inspired discipline, integrity, and respect across generations.

To transform psychiatry, activists must embody those same principles: combine fierce dedication to human rights with rigorous intellectual clarity, personal integrity, and genuine empathy. We must continue to demand a system that honors human dignity, respects bodily autonomy, and recognizes the inherent capacity of every individual to heal.

Thompson: After that first, very active period between 1986 and 2001, I never completely left the movement. The last 25 years have been characterized by a constant focus on psychiatric issues and ongoing contact with various people, including activists.

I also recently got in touch with a psychologist and a TAO (Threat Assessment Officer), and now this connection suggests a possible political initiative that could be more promising than anything I have been involved in since, sadly, the initial promise of the advocacy movement began to fade at the turn of the century.

One of the reasons for my reduced activity—if not my diminished attention and interest—has been my view that the advocacy community, whilst never lacking in integrity or commitment, has, in my opinion, never developed the best political strategies.

On a more personal level, when I am not dealing with or thinking about issues relating to the defense of psychiatric rights, I spend a great deal of time reading and reflecting on current and past history, about which I have written. And ever since my wife and I realized we shared a passion for travel, we have taken countless trips over the last 40 years, which have taken us, quite literally, all over the world.

Thompson: It has been my pleasure, Alan. Thank you.

author: Xiaofan Yue
title: Two Decades After China’s Internet-Addiction Scandals, Why Does Coercive “Treatment” Keep Coming Back?
content:
I

n May 2026, a 21-year-old man (pseudonym Liang Yu) was ambushed in Guizhou by three men posing as cyber-security officials. They forced him into a van, tied him down, and hauled him across provincial lines to a closed disciplinary school in Chongqing. His parents had paid roughly 30,000 yuan just to fix his habit of staying up late. While these institutions promise to cure “internet addiction” and behavioral problems, 

what actually waited for Liang Yu were violent beatings and a failed attempt to escape

.







In October 2017, the 

South China Morning Post

 reported that students at the Jiangxi-based “internet addiction” school were subjected to physical punishment, confinement, and other forms of abuse. 

Radio Free Asia

 soon followed with reports of beatings, forced labor, and severe physical restriction. By 2019, 

SupChina

 (later 

The China Project

) revisited the case after activists who exposed the school began receiving death threats. 

Voice of America

 later cited Yuzhang Academy as a prime example of China’s broader disciplinary school system, pointing out cases of illegal detention, physical abuse, and student self-harm.




English-language Chinese outlets also covered the case in detail. 

Caixin Global’s 

2017 investigation reported on solitary confinement, beatings, forced labor, and how some students were tricked or forcibly taken to the school

author: Nina Garcia Steel
title: Crossing Dimensions of Pain Without Losing My Soul
content:
A

s I sit here in my—as I like to call it—Oasis in the Desert, looking out my window at the morning clouds gloriously dancing to the tune the songbirds sing every morning is simply a treasure. I can smile at the sun and sway with the wind as it tickles my senses. I enjoy this morning view as I sip a cup of sweet herbal tea and take in the rays of light.




There was a time when such treasures were absent in my mind. I was living with undeniable pain that I could not explain, except in my poetry.




Photo by Nina Garcia Steel




It’s my heart that aches the most.




The feeling of nerves tearing and bones slowly breaking.




Flares of fire running through my veins.




The words that everyone took as metaphorical were literal words of agony from trauma that started decades earlier. It would take over half a century to discover the root cause of the autoimmune conditions that developed, the near dementia scares. At one point, I was having severe neurological attacks where I lost control of my limbs entirely, making them feel as though they were being tossed around like a rag doll. I picked three alcoholic husbands and stayed in abusive relationships. Little did I know that all of this was coming from the same place: 

unprocessed trauma

.




It took me by surprise too. I had been making decisions about who I chose to be my mate based on what I thought was normal from what

author: James Moore
title: Be More Human: Why Mental Health Care is Broken and What We Can Do to Fix It: An Interview with Sir Norman Lamb
content:
Hello, this is James and welcome to the Mad in America podcast. This week, we are asking why people with mental health conditions die 15-20 years earlier than people without. Why does the UK spend £100 million every year placing patients far from home? How did the question, ‘What matters to you?’ transform mental health care in Norway? Can mental healthcare be more compassionate?

Sir Norman Lamb asks these questions, and more, in his book Be More Human, published by Jessica Kingsley Publishers. Sir Norman is a former Health Minister, an NHS trust chair, and a dedicated mental health campaigner who was knighted in 2019 for his public and political service. He has seen the cracks in the system up close. In his book, he sets out to answer these questions, and many others, uncovering the reasons why our mental health services are failing. He shares eye-opening stories from patients who have been let down, but also inspiring tales from trailblazers who are shaking things up with creative, community-first solutions.

In this interview, we talk about how his personal and professional experiences led to him wanting to lift the lid on the UK’s mental health system. We also discuss how personal accounts of mistreatment and abuse motivated him to think differently about the human element so often missing from mental healthcare. author: Marion Brown
title: A Decade of the Rise and Rise of “Functional Neurological Disorder” (FND)
content:
“FND occurs when the brain has difficulty sending and receiving signals properly, even though scans like MRI or CT appear normal. It affects movement, sensation, speech, cognition, and other functions. Symptoms are genuine, involuntary, and can be disabling.”




—

NIH website




M

ore and more people are being diagnosed with ‘functional neurological disorder’ (FND). FND is essentially a term for ‘unexplained’ symptoms—including severely disabling symptoms such as movement disorders, blackouts and so-called ‘non-epileptic seizures’—and which doctors say has no clear cause. I began to notice about 10 years ago that these ‘unexplained’ symptoms were the same symptoms as those experienced by some people when taking prescribed drugs for ‘depression’, ‘anxiety’, ‘stress’, etc. and especially when trying to reduce or come off these psychiatric drugs.




I began to meet more and more people with the FND diagnosis who were also experiencing withdrawal effects after stopping antidepressants, benzodiazepines, and other psychiatric drugs—but no doctors seemed to connect the two. author: Poetry Collection
title: Reality Kicks by Terese Blåklokke
content:
Learning the truth
can tear you apart
wrench your guts
and change 
	your heart

the solution is simple
but hard to complete
you must 
	let it rip
and reap the wheat

you must welcome 
	the actual
braincrunching fact
that the «experts» 
	you trust
are all part 
	of an act

they’re playing 
	their parts
as government tools
not knowing they too
are brainwashed 
	fools

«this poet is joking
she’s surely sarcastic»
you laugh 
	as your brain
turns more 
	into plastic




* * *




After over 20 years of battling the symptoms, Terese Blåklokke has overcome the struggles of her illness “schizoaffective disorder” through faith, art, poetry, food, intensive introspection and mental training. Today, when an official “expert” claims to present facts, she is quick to search elsewhere for the actual solutions – as that has been where she most often has found hers.

Reality Kicks by Terese Blåklokke

author: Justin Garson
title: Seeing BPD in a Positive Light: An Interview with Dr. Shay Welch
content:
P

eople often take psychiatric drugs because there’s something about themselves they don’t like—extreme low mood, threatening voices, or panic attacks. But many who’ve been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD) take drugs for the sake of others. They’re repeatedly told that their very personalities are disordered, pathological or just intolerable. This message is profoundly stigmatizing. It can contribute to isolation, loneliness, and even suicidal thoughts.




In September 2024, I talked with 

Dr. Shay Welch

, a philosophy professor at Spelman College. Welch, who’s been diagnosed with BPD, truly writes from an insider’s perspective—a perspective that’s nearly absent from the academic literature.




Shay Welch




Her recent paper, “

Am I Safe Enough for You Now? BPD and the Forced Erasure of Personal Identity

,” describes how people with BPD often feel forced to erase who they are to make others feel safe. We discuss ways of promoting more positive messaging around BPD, and creating a more tolerant and accepting society.




The title of her paper captures a theme that ran throughout our conversation: “treatment” for BPD is often less about alleviating the diagnosed person’s suffering than about making them more tolerable to other people. When I studied 30 consecutive cases from Denmark

3

author: Anne-Marie Cicala
title: How My Body Rejected Lithium After 25 Years
content:
It was two o’clock in the morning on our first night out of town in New Orleans, and I woke up suddenly in the dark hotel room feeling horribly sick and needing to run to the bathroom. What ensued was messy and lasted for two hours. I kept waking up with my head in the toilet to do it again. I used most of the towels in the bathroom to clean up both myself and the mess I had made on the floor. At 4am, exhausted and beyond tired, not knowing exactly how to handle the situation, I opened my hotel room door completely naked, threw the armful of soiled towels into the hallway and went back to bed.

The next morning, I woke up extremely nauseous. I was thankful we had packed a decent amount of THC gummies, as they proved to be a savior for the next few days. The gummies took the nausea down to a level where I was able to function throughout the day, but I was still not feeling right or well. I didn’t know if it was from the previous night’s events, but I felt subdued by a heavy brain fog.

author: Donald Zrebiec
title: She Was Here: Finding My Grandmother After Willard
content:
I

 often mention that I was the only one of Catherine Smoral’s grandchildren to see her alive. I was six years old, and the visit to Willard State Hospital was a bad experience for all four of us who were there: my mother Anna, my Uncle Tony, me, and my grandmother Catherine. The three of us who came from Syracuse were all shocked at the physical and mental condition of our mother and grandmother. Our visit upset her, and we spent a very short time there before being asked to leave.




My grandmother was born in Poland in 1884. She emigrated to the U.S. in 1900, and in 1902 she married my grandfather, Karol Smoral. They were married at Sacred Heart, a beautiful Polish church that still stands on the west side of Syracuse. They were a happy couple who went on to have nine children, a happy and healthy brood. Karol bought his own home on Morgan Avenue, and a family burial plot at Sacred Heart Cemetery not far from it. In the early 1920s, disaster struck the household.




I received, I believe from Ancestry.com, a copy of an article from the Syracuse Herald from the early 1920s. This is how it read:




SMORAL FAMILY WOES CULMINATE IN COMMITTAL OF EIGHT TO INSTITUTIONS. Mother and Son Are Sent to Willard. Six Younger Children to Various Orphanages. Father Died in December.

title: The Process: Helen Wesnes Fights for Her Rights
content:

Mad in Norway

Helen Wesnes took control of her own case from the beginning and has already won several victories in the legal system. She does this for all those who lose their lives in psychiatry. Photo: private




H




elen Wesnes was 19 when she sought help from the health care system. It cost her 15 years, followed by a 12-year legal process. She has already won millions in damages and is ready for the next round. Now she explains how she built her case.




Few people know that in Norway there is a society within a society, full of paradoxes and with no known way out. This is the Norway offered to psychiatric patients once they fall under the Mental Health Care Act. “Someone must have slandered Josef K., for one morning, without having done anything wrong, he was arrested,” writes Franz Kafka in his world-famous 

The Trial

, and what follows is a nightmare about the individual’s powerlessness against the arbitrariness of bureaucracy. Josef K. and Helen W. don’t have a great deal in common, since she walked out alive and victorious. Otherwise, the process was much the same.




“The media are failing their mission when they don’t raise this case to a systemic level. The practice itself is the problem, not whatever diagnosis the patient may have.”

author: Rupinder Legha, MD
title: From Eradicating Psychosis to Being With Voices: A Psychiatrist’s Journey from Biomedical Nihilism to Experiences of Humanity
content:
A

s a double-board-certified child, adolescent, and adult psychiatrist with nearly twenty years of experience treating “mental illness” worldwide, I have attended more mental health conferences than I can count. Nowhere is the tension higher than when the conversation turns to “schizophrenia” and “psychotic disorders.” Putting people with lived experience, family members of those labeled unwell, and clinicians in the same room for the sake of meaningful dialogue can sour fast. The purported goal of determining how best to support and assess a person can quickly shift to how to manage and control them. Someone inevitably insists there is no other way than meds and, if needed, forced “care.”




Four Conversations at Once




Amidst the cacophony, I sometimes have nothing to say, sensing that jumping in might only make things worse. The stakes always seem high for everyone in the room, the emotional charge palpable.




We might hear from people subjected to psychiatric coercion from childhood onward because of the voices they lived with, forced to submit to a construction of mental illness requiring involuntary hospitalizations and medications, and to culturally unsound formulations that pathologized them rather than looking for their meaning and value.

author: Konstantinos Kontis
title: The Psychotherapist as a Paid “Fantasy-Friend”: The Taboo of Money and Payment in Therapy
content:
T

his text consists of a series of reflections that arose and developed from two events—one personal, the other relayed to me—concerning the act of payment in psychotherapy as well as the therapists’ own attitudes toward it.




The two incidents are the following:







My psychotherapist was quite clear and strict. Payment is made in cash at the end of the session—50 euros—and it’s best to have the exact amount. One day I had 60 euros (I can’t recall the reason for this “oversight” of mine), which obviously would have required her to give me 10 euros in change. At the time of payment, when I showed her the three 20-euro bills and told her that unfortunately I didn’t have the exact amount, I noticed an expression of obvious uneasiness on her face as she hurriedly opened her wallet and handed me the change for this transaction. This reaction struck me as particularly odd, as if she preferred to avoid such minor interactions in her psychotherapeutic practice.




The following incident was communicated to me by a friend. During a session in a psychoanalytic training program, the training psychoanalyst noted that payment in psychotherapy is of the utmost importance and must always be required. author: Chandra Bozelko
title: I’m Done With Mental Health Providers
content:
B

ack in the early 2000s, my parents had me involuntarily hospitalized several times. I got the whole psychiatric smorgasbord: strapped to a gurney when I was perfectly able to walk, injected with medications against my will, 

spoken slowly and loudly to

 like I was incapacitated. I got the works, except for one hallmark experience of forcible treatment: I was never restrained because I didn’t do anything to endanger anyone. When people ask me why I didn’t kick or punch the nurse administering the shots, I don’t have a good answer. I’m just not good at violence.




The psychiatrists are, though. They never physically struck me — with all the damage they inflicted, they didn’t need to — but I saw one esteemed Yale shrink throw a red-haired woman onto a couch.




Because I criticized the system and I wouldn’t agree to debilitating regimens of medications, I was labeled as having no insight into my own illness. That’s worse than any diagnosis they can muster. To them, I was so ill that even the most severe psychiatric interventions would never help me. One famed Columbia doctor told my parents to abandon me, like leave me stranded there in New York, because I was terminally mentally ill.
